entries.5ea10b9875b37d73f6a49d97c8ee0d6c8574280b: <div sID="gen17595" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Jer.18" sID="Jer.18"/> <div eID="gen17595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17596" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17597" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A general declaration of God's ways in dealing with nations and kingdoms, that he can easily do what he will with them, as easily as the potter can with the clay (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.18.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), but that he certainly will do what is just and fair with them. If he threaten their ruin, yet upon their repentance he will return in mercy to them, and, when he is coming towards them in mercy, nothing but their sin will stop the progress of his favours, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.7-Jer.18.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. II. A particular demonstration of the folly of the men of Judah and Jerusalem in departing from their God to idols, and so bringing ruin upon themselves notwithstanding the fair warnings given them and God's kind intentions towards them, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.11-Jer.18.17">ver. 11-17</reference>. III. The prophet's complaint to God of the base ingratitude and unreasonable malice of his enemies, persecutors, and slanderers, and his prayers against them, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18-Jer.18.23">ver. 18-23</reference>.
entries.99cd6279598893b495ceac4b0bd3802439d93d81: <div eID="gen17597" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17596" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sovereign Prerogative of God; Divine Goodness and Equity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen17598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word which came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to me, saying, <hi type="super">6</hi> O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Behold, as the clay <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the potter's hand, so <hi type="italic">are</hi> ye in mine hand, O house of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">At what</hi> instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy <hi type="italic">it;</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them. <hi type="super">9</hi> And <hi type="italic">at what</hi> instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant <hi type="italic">it;</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them. <div eID="gen17598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17599" type="x-p"/> The prophet is here sent to <hi type="italic">the potter's house</hi> (he knew where to find it), not to preach a sermon as before to the gates of Jerusalem, but to prepare a sermon, or rather to receive it ready prepared. Those needed not to study their sermons that had them, as he had this, by immediate inspiration. "<hi type="italic">Go to the potter's house,</hi> and observe how he manages his work, and there <hi type="italic">I will cause thee,</hi> by silent whispers, <hi type="italic">to hear my words.</hi> There thou shalt receive a message, to be delivered to the people." Note, Those that would know God's mind must observe his appointments, and attend where they may hear his words. The prophet was never <hi type="italic">disobedient to the heavenly vision,</hi> and therefore went to the potter's house (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.3">v. 3</reference>) and took notice how he <hi type="italic">wrought his work upon the wheels,</hi> just as he pleased, with a great deal of ease, and in a little time. And (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.4">v. 4</reference>) when a lump of clay that he designed to form into one shape either proved too stiff, or had a stone in it, or some way or other came to be <hi type="italic">marred in his hand,</hi> he presently turned it into another shape; if it will not serve for a vessel of honour, it will serve for a vessel of dishonour, just <hi type="italic">as seems good to the potter.</hi> It is probable that Jeremiah knew well enough how the potter wrought his work, and how easily he threw it into what form he pleased; but he must go and observe it <hi type="italic">now,</hi> that, having the idea of it fresh in his mind, he might the more readily and distinctly apprehend that truth which God designed thereby to represent to him, and might the more intelligently explain it to the people. God <hi type="italic">used similitudes by his servants the prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.10">Hos. xii. 10</reference>), and it was requisite that they should themselves understand the similitudes they used. Ministers will make a good use of their converse with the business and affairs of this life if they learn thereby to speak more plainly and familiarly to people about the things of God, and to expound scripture comparisons. For they ought to make all their knowledge some way or other serviceable to their profession. <div eID="gen17599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17600" type="x-p"/> Now let us see what the message is which Jeremiah receives, and is entrusted with the delivery of, at the potter's house. While he looks carefully upon the potter's work, God darts into his mind these two great truths, which he must preach to <hi type="italic">the house of Israel:</hi>— <div eID="gen17600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17601" type="x-p"/> I. That God has both an incontestable authority and an irresistible ability to form and fashion kingdoms and nations as he pleases, so as to serve his own purposes: "<hi type="italic">Cannot I do with you as this potter, saith the Lord?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">v. 6</reference>. Have not I as absolute a power over you in respect both of might and of right?" Nay, God has a clearer title to a dominion over us than the potter has over the clay; for the potter only gives it its form, whereas we have both matter and form from God. <hi type="italic">As the clay is in the potter's hand</hi> to be moulded and shaped as he pleases, <hi type="italic">so are you in my hand.</hi> This intimates, 1. That God has an incontestable sovereignty over us, is not debtor to us, may dispose of us as he thinks fit, and is not accountable to us, and that it would be as absurd for us to dispute this as for the clay to quarrel with the potter. 2. That it is a very easy thing with God to make what use he pleases of us and what changes he pleases with us, and that we cannot resist him. One turn of the hand, one turn of the wheel, quite alters the shape of the clay, makes it a vessel, unmakes it, new-makes it. Thus are our times in God's hand, and not in our own, and it is in vain for us to strive with him. It is spoken here of nations; the most politic, the most potent, are what God is pleased to make them, and no other. See this explained by Job (<reference osisRef="Job.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">He increaseth the nations and destroyeth them; he enlargeth the nations and straiteneth them again.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33">Ps. cvii. 33</reference>, &c., and compare <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">All nations before God are as the drop of the bucket,</hi> soon wiped away, <hi type="italic">or the small dust of the balance,</hi> soon blown away (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa. xl. 15</reference>), and therefore, no doubt, as easily managed as the clay by the potter. 3. That God will not be a loser by any in his glory, at long run, but, if he be not glorified by them, he will be glorified upon them. If the potter's vessel be marred for one use, it shall serve for another; those that will not be monuments of mercy shall be monuments of justice. <hi type="italic">The Lord has made all things for himself, yea, even the wicked for the day of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Prov. xvi. 4</reference>. God formed us out of the clay (<reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job xxxiii. 6</reference>), nay, and we are still as clay in his hands (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">Isa. lxiv. 8</reference>); and has not he the same power over us that the potter has over the clay? (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">Rom. ix. 21</reference>), and are not we bound to submit, as the clay to the potter's wisdom and will? <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15-Isa.29.16">Isa. xxix. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">xlv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen17601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17602" type="x-p"/> II. That, in the exercise of this authority and ability, he always goes by fixed rules of equity and goodness. He dispenses favours indeed in a way of sovereignty, but never punishes by arbitrary power. <hi type="italic">High is his right hand,</hi> yet he rules not with a <hi type="italic">high hand,</hi> but, as it follows there, <hi type="italic">Justice and judgment are the habitation of his throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.13-Ps.89.14">Ps. lxxxix. 13, 14</reference>. God asserts his despotic power, and tells us what he might do, but at the same time assures us that he will act as a righteous and merciful Judge. 1. When God is coming against us in ways of judgment we may be sure that it is for our sins, which shall appear by this, that national repentance will stop the progress of the judgments (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.7-Jer.18.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">If God speak concerning a nation to pluck up</hi> its fences that secure it, and so lay it open, its fruit-trees that adorn and enrich it, and so leave it desolate—to pull down its fortifications, that the enemy may have liberty to enter in, its habitations, that the inhabitants may be under a necessity of going out, and so <hi type="italic">destroy it</hi> as either a vineyard or a city is destroyed—in this case, if <hi type="italic">that nation</hi> take the alarm, repent of their sins and reform their lives, turn every one from his evil way and return to God, God will graciously accept them, will not proceed in his controversy, will return in mercy to them, and, though he cannot change his mind, he will change his way, so that it may be said, He <hi type="italic">repents him of the evil he said he would do to them.</hi> Thus often in the time of the Judges, when the oppressed people were penitent people, still God raised them up saviours; and, when they turned to God, their affairs immediately took a new turn. It was Nineveh's case, and we wish it had oftener been Jerusalem's; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.14">2 Chron. vii. 14</reference>. It is an undoubted truth that a sincere conversion from the evil of sin will be an effectual prevention of the evil of punishment; and God can as easily raise up a penitent people from their ruins as the potter can make anew the vessel of clay when it was <hi type="italic">marred in his hand.</hi> 2. When God is coming towards us in ways of mercy, if any stop be given to the progress of that mercy, it is nothing but sin that gives it (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.9-Jer.18.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">If God speak concerning a nation to build and to plant it,</hi> to advance and establish all the true interests of it, it is <hi type="italic">his husbandly</hi> and <hi type="italic">his building</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1 Cor. iii. 9</reference>), and, if he speak in favour of it, it is done, it is increased, it is enriched, it is enlarged, its trade flourishes, its government is settled in good hands, and all its affairs prosper and its enterprises succeed. But if this nation, which God is thus loading with benefits, <hi type="italic">do evil in his sight</hi> and <hi type="italic">obey not his voice,</hi>—if it lose its virtue, and become debauched and profane,—if religion grow into contempt, and vice to get to be fashionable, and so be kept in countenance and reputation, and there be a general decay of serious godliness among them,—then God will turn his hand against them, will pluck up what he was planting, and pull down what he was building (<reference osisRef="Jer.45.4">ch. xlv. 4</reference>); the good work that was in the doing shall stand still and be let fall, and what favours were further designed shall be withheld; and this is called his <hi type="italic">repenting of the good wherewith he said he would benefit them,</hi> as he changed his purpose concerning Eli's house (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1 Sam. ii. 30</reference>) and hurried Israel back into the wilderness when he had brought them within sight of Canaan. Note, Sin is the great mischief-maker between God and a people; it forfeits the benefit of his promises and spoils the success of their prayers. It defeats his kind intentions concerning them (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Hos. vii. 1</reference>) and baffles their pleasing expectations from him. It ruins their comforts, prolongs their grievances, brings them into straits, and retards their deliverances, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.1-Isa.59.2">Isa. lix. 1, 2</reference>.
entries.133000d5010312b7f57a5a89f4d0a97b43502c5f: <div eID="gen17602" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">People of God Accused and Threatened; Folly of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen17603" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Ask ye now among the heathen, who hath heard such things: the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing. <hi type="super">14</hi> Will <hi type="italic">a man</hi> leave the snow of Lebanon <hi type="italic">which cometh</hi> from the rock of the field? <hi type="italic">or</hi> shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken? <hi type="super">15</hi> Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways <hi type="italic">from</hi> the ancient paths, to walk in paths, <hi type="italic">in</hi> a way not cast up; <hi type="super">16</hi> To make their land desolate, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a perpetual hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, and wag his head. <hi type="super">17</hi> I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy; I will shew them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity. <div eID="gen17603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17604" type="x-p"/> These verses seem to be the application of the general truths laid down in the foregoing part of the chapter to the nation of the Jews and their present state. <div eID="gen17604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17605" type="x-p"/> I. God was now speaking concerning them <hi type="italic">to pluck up,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to pull down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to destroy;</hi> for it is that part of the rule of judgment that their case agrees with (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Go, and tell</hi> them" (saith God), "<hi type="italic">Behold I frame evil against you and devise against you.</hi> Providence in all its operations is plainly working towards your ruin. Look upon your conduct towards God, and you cannot but see that you deserve it; look upon his dealings with you, and you cannot but see that he designs it." He frames evil, as the potter frames the vessel, so as to answer the end. <div eID="gen17605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17606" type="x-p"/> II. He invites them by repentance and reformation to meet him in the way of his judgments and so to prevent his further proceedings against them: "<hi type="italic">Return you now every one from his evil ways,</hi> that so (according to the rule before laid down) God may turn from the evil he had purported to do unto you, and that providence which seemed to be framed like a vessel on the wheel against you shall immediately be thrown into a new shape, and the issue shall be in favour of you." Note, The warnings of God's word, and the threatenings of his providence, should be improved by us as strong inducements to us to reform our lives, in which it is not enough to <hi type="italic">turn from our evil ways,</hi> but we must <hi type="italic">make our ways and our doings good,</hi> conformable to the rule, to the law. <div eID="gen17606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17607" type="x-p"/> III. He foresees their obstinacy, and their perverse refusal to comply with this invitation, though it tended so much to their own benefit (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They said, "There is no hope.</hi> If we must not be delivered unless we return from our evil ways, we may even despair of ever being delivered, for we are resolved that <hi type="italic">we will walk after our own devices.</hi> It is to no purpose for the prophets to say any more to us, to use any more arguments, or to press the matter any further; we will have our way, whatever it cost us; <hi type="italic">we will do every one the imagination of his</hi> own <hi type="italic">evil heart,</hi> and will not be under the restraint of the divine law." Note, That which ruins sinners is affecting to live as they list. They call it liberty to live at large; whereas for a man to be a slave to his lusts is the worst of slaveries. See how strangely some men's hearts are hardened by the deceitfulness of sin that they will not so much as promise amendment; nay, they set the judgments of God at defiance: "We will go on with <hi type="italic">our own devices,</hi> and let God go on with his; and we will venture the issue." <div eID="gen17607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17608" type="x-p"/> IV. He upbraids them with the monstrous folly of their obstinacy, and their hating to be reformed. Surely never were people guilty of such an absurdity, never any that pretended to reason acted so unreasonably (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ask you among the heathen,</hi> even those that had not the benefit of divine revelation, no oracles, no prophets, as Judah and Jerusalem had, yet, even among them, <hi type="italic">who hath heard such a thing?</hi> The Ninevites, when thus warned, turned from their evil ways. Some of the worst of men, when they are told of their faults, especially when they begin to smart for them, will at least promise reformation and say that they will endeavour to mend. But <hi type="italic">the virgin of Israel</hi> bids defiance to repentance, is resolved to go on frowardly, whatever conscience and Providence say to the contrary, and thus <hi type="italic">has done a horrible thing.</hi> She should have preserved herself pure and chaste for God, who had espoused her to himself; but she has alienated herself from him, and refuses to return to him. Note, It is <hi type="italic">a horrible thing,</hi> enough to make one tremble to think of it, that those who have made their condition sad by sinning should make it desperate by refusing to reform. Wilful impenitence is the grossest self-murder; and that is <hi type="italic">a horrible thing,</hi> which we should abhor the thought of. <div eID="gen17608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17609" type="x-p"/> V. He shows their folly in two things:— <div eID="gen17609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17610" type="x-p"/> 1. In the nature of the sin itself that they were guilty of. They forsook God for idols, which was the most horrible thing that could be, for they put a most dangerous cheat upon themselves (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.14-Jer.18.15">v. 14, 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will a</hi> thirsty traveller <hi type="italic">leave the snow,</hi> which, being melted, runs down from the mountains <hi type="italic">of Lebanon,</hi> and, passing over <hi type="italic">the rock of the field,</hi> flows in clear, clean, crystal streams? Will he leave these, pass these by, and think to better himself with some dirty puddle-water? <hi type="italic">Or shall the cold flowing waters that come from any other place be forsaken</hi> in the heat of summer? No; when men are parched with heat and drought, and meet with cooling refreshing streams, they will make use of them, and not turn their backs upon them. The margin reads it, "<hi type="italic">Will a man</hi> that is travelling the road <hi type="italic">leave my fields,</hi> which are plain and level, <hi type="italic">for a rock,</hi> which is rough and hard, <hi type="italic">or for the snow of Lebanon,</hi> which, lying in great drifts, makes the road impassable? <hi type="italic">Or shall the running waters be forsaken for the strange cold waters?</hi> No; in these things men know when they are well off, and will keep so; they will not leave a certainty for an uncertainty. But <hi type="italic">my people have forgotten me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">v. 15</reference>), have quitted <hi type="italic">a fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. They have burnt incense to</hi> idols, that are as vain as <hi type="italic">vanity</hi> itself, that are not what they pretend to be nor can perform what is expected from them." They had not the common wit of travellers, but even their leaders caused them to err, and they were content to be misled. (1.) They left <hi type="italic">the ancient paths,</hi> which were appointed by the divine law, which had been walked in by all the saints, which were therefore the right way to their journey's end, a safe way, and, being well-tracked, were both easy to hit and easy to walk in. But, when they were advised to keep to the good old way, they positively said that they would not, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">ch. vi. 16</reference>. (2.) They chose by-paths; they walked <hi type="italic">in a way not cast up,</hi> not in the highway, the King's highway, in which they might travel safely, and which would certainly lead them to their right end, but in a dirty way, a rough way, a way in which they could not but <hi type="italic">stumble;</hi> such was the way of idolatry (such is the way of all iniquity—it is a false way, it is a way full of stumbling-blocks) and yet this way they chose to walk in and lead others in. <div eID="gen17610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17611" type="x-p"/> 2. In the mischievous consequences of it. Though the thing itself were bad, they might have had some excuse for it if they could have promised themselves any good out of it. But the direct tendency of it was <hi type="italic">to make their land desolate, and,</hi> consequently, themselves miserable (for so the inhabitants must needs be if their country be laid waste), and both themselves and their land <hi type="italic">a perpetual hissing.</hi> Those deserve to be hissed that have fair warning given them and will not take it. <hi type="italic">Every one that passes by</hi> their land shall make his remarks upon it, and <hi type="italic">shall be astonished, and way his head,</hi> some wondering, others commiserating, others triumphing in the desolations of a country that had been <hi type="italic">the glory of all lands.</hi> They shall wag their heads in derision, upbraiding them with their folly in forsaking God and their duty, and so pulling this misery upon their own heads. Note, Those that revolt from God will justly be made the scorn of all about them, and, having reproached the Lord, will themselves be a reproach. <hi type="italic">Their land</hi> being made <hi type="italic">desolate,</hi> in pursuance of their destruction, it is threatened (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will scatter them as with an east wind,</hi> which is fierce and violent; by it they shall be hurried to and fro <hi type="italic">before the enemy,</hi> and find no way open to escape. They shall not only flee before the enemy (that they might do and yet make an orderly retreat), but they shall be scattered, some one way and some another. That which completes their misery is, <hi type="italic">I will show them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.</hi> Our calamities may be easily borne if God look towards us, and smile upon us, when we are under them, if he countenance us and show us favour; but if he turn <hi type="italic">the back</hi> upon us, if he show himself displeased, if he be deaf to our prayers and refuse us his help, if he forsake us, leave us to ourselves, and stand at a distance from us, we are quite undone. <hi type="italic">If he hide his face, who then can behold him?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>. Herein God would deal with them as they had dealt with him (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">ch. ii. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">They have turned their back unto me, and not their face.</hi> It is a righteous thing with God to show himself strange to those in the day of their trouble who have shown themselves rude and undutiful to him in their prosperity. This will have its full accomplishment in that day when God will say to those who, though they have been professors of piety, were yet workers of iniquity, <hi type="italic">Depart from me, I know you not,</hi> nay, <hi type="italic">I never knew you.</hi>
entries.606dccb125eda2f5e59f748815df5483d4e734e6: <div eID="gen17611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conduct of Persecutors; Prophetic Imprecations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen17612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then said they, Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words. <hi type="super">19</hi> Give heed to me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and hearken to the voice of them that contend with me. <hi type="super">20</hi> Shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to turn away thy wrath from them. <hi type="super">21</hi> Therefore deliver up their children to the famine, and pour out their <hi type="italic">blood</hi> by the force of the sword; and let their wives be bereaved of their children, and <hi type="italic">be</hi> widows; and let their men be put to death; <hi type="italic">let</hi> their young men <hi type="italic">be</hi> slain by the sword in battle. <hi type="super">22</hi> Let a cry be heard from their houses, when thou shalt bring a troop suddenly upon them: for they have digged a pit to take me, and hid snares for my feet. <hi type="super">23</hi> Yet, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou knowest all their counsel against me to slay <hi type="italic">me:</hi> forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight, but let them be overthrown before thee; deal <hi type="italic">thus</hi> with them in the time of thine anger. <div eID="gen17612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17613" type="x-p"/> The prophet here, as sometimes before, brings in his own affairs, but very much for instruction to us. <div eID="gen17613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17614" type="x-p"/> I. See here what are the common methods of the persecutors. We may see this in Jeremiah's enemies, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">v. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen17614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17615" type="x-p"/> 1. They laid their heads together to consult what they should do against him, both to be revenged on him for what he had said and to stop his mouth for the future: <hi type="italic">They said, Come and let us devise devices against Jeremiah.</hi> The enemies of God's people and ministers have been often very crafty themselves, and confederate with one another, to do them mischief. What they cannot act to the prejudice of religion separately they will try to do in concert. <hi type="italic">The wicked plots against the just.</hi> Caiaphas, and the chief priests and elders, did so against our blessed Saviour himself. The opposition which the gates of hell give to the kingdom of heaven is carried on with a great deal of cursed policy. God had said (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">I devise a device against you;</hi> and now, as if they resolved to be quits with him and to outwit Infinite Wisdom itself, they resolve to <hi type="italic">devise devices against</hi> God's prophet, not only against his person, but against the word he delivered to them, which they thought by their subtle management to defeat. O the prodigious madness of those that hope to disannul God's counsel! <div eID="gen17615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17616" type="x-p"/> 2. Herein they pretended a mighty zeal for the church, which, they suggested, was in danger if Jeremiah was tolerated to preach as he did: "<hi type="italic">Come,</hi>" say they, "let us silence and crush him, <hi type="italic">for the law shall not perish from the priest; the law of truth is in their mouths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.6">Mal. ii. 6</reference>) and there we will seek it; the administration of ordinances according to the law is in their hands, and neither the one nor the other shall be wrested from them. <hi type="italic">Counsel shall not perish from the wise;</hi> the administration of public affairs shall always be lodged with the privy-counsellors and ministers of state, to whom it belongs; <hi type="italic">nor</hi> shall <hi type="italic">the word</hi> perish <hi type="italic">from the prophets</hi>" —they mean those of their own choosing, who prophesied to them smooth things, and flattered them with visions of peace. Two things they insinuated:—(1.) That Jeremiah could not be himself a true prophet, but was a pretender and a usurper, because he neither was commissioned by the priests, nor concurred with the other prophets, whose authority therefore will be despised if he be suffered to go on. "If Jeremiah be regarded as an oracle, farewell the reputation of our priests, our wise men, and prophets; but <hi type="italic">that</hi> must be supported, which is reason enough why he must be suppressed." (2.) That the matter of his prophecies could not be from God, because it reflected sometimes upon the prophets and priests; he had charged them with being the ringleaders of all the mischief (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">ch. v. 31</reference>) and deceiving the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">ch. xiv. 14</reference>); he had foretold that their <hi type="italic">heart should perish,</hi> and <hi type="italic">be astonished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.9">ch. iv. 9</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the wise men should be dismayed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.9-Jer.8.10">ch. viii. 9, 10</reference>), that the priests and prophets should be intoxicated, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">ch. xiii. 13</reference>. Now this galled them more than any thing else. Presuming upon the promise of God's presence with their priests and prophets, they could not believe that he would ever leave them. The guides of the church must needs be infallible, and therefore he who foretold their being infatuated must be condemned as a false prophet. Thus, under colour of zeal for the church, have its best friends been run down. <div eID="gen17616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17617" type="x-p"/> 3. They agreed to do all they could to blast his reputation: "<hi type="italic">Come, let us smite him with the tongue,</hi> put him into an ill name, fasten a bad character upon him, represent him to some as despicable and fit to be prosecuted, to all as odious and not fit to be tolerated." This was their device, <hi type="italic">fortiter calumniari, aliquid adhærebit—to throw the vilest calumnies at him, in hopes that some would adhere to him.</hi> to dress him up in bearskins, otherwise they could not bait him. Those who projected this, it is likely, were men of figure, whose tongue was no small slander, whose representations, though ever so false, would be credited both by princes and people, to make him obnoxious to the justice of the one and the fury of the other. The scourge of such tongues will give not only smart lashes, but deep wounds; it is a great mercy therefore to be <hi type="italic">hidden from it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.21">Job v. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen17617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17618" type="x-p"/> 4. To set others an example, they resolved that they would not themselves regard any thing he said, though it appeared ever so weighty and ever so well confirmed as a message from God: <hi type="italic">Let us not give heed to any of his words;</hi> for, right or wrong, they will look upon them to be <hi type="italic">his words,</hi> and not the words of God. What good can be done with those who hear the word of God with a resolution not to heed it or believe it? Nay, <div eID="gen17618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17619" type="x-p"/> 5. That they may effectually silence him, they resolve to be the death of him (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">All their counsel against me</hi> is <hi type="italic">to slay me.</hi> They <hi type="italic">hunt for the precious life;</hi> and a precious life indeed it was that they hunted for. Long was this Jerusalem's wretched character, <hi type="italic">Thou that killedst</hi> many of <hi type="italic">the prophets,</hi> and wouldst have killed them all. <div eID="gen17619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17620" type="x-p"/> II. See here what is the common relief of the persecuted. This we may see in the course that Jeremiah took when he met with this hard usage. He immediately applied to his God by prayer, and so gave himself ease. <div eID="gen17620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17621" type="x-p"/> 1. He referred himself and his cause to God's cognizance, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.19">v. 19</reference>. They would not regard a word he said, would not admit his complaints, nor take any notice of his grievances; but, <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> (says he), <hi type="italic">do thou give heed to me.</hi> It is matter of comfort to faithful ministers that, if men will not give heed to their praying. He appeals to God as an impartial Judge, that will hear both sides, as every judge ought to do. "Do not only <hi type="italic">give heed to me,</hi> but <hi type="italic">hearken to the voice of those that contend with me;</hi> hear what they have to say against me and for themselves, and then make it to appear that thou <hi type="italic">sittest in the throne, judging right.</hi> Hear the voice of my contenders, how noisy and clamorous they are, how false and malicious all they say is, and let them be <hi type="italic">judged out of their own mouth; cause their own tongues to fall upon them.</hi>" <div eID="gen17621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17622" type="x-p"/> 2. He complains of their base ingratitude to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall evil be recompensed for good,</hi> and shall it go unpunished? Wilt not thou recompense me good for that evil?" <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.12">2 Sam. xvi. 12</reference>. To render good for good is human, evil for evil is brutish, good for evil is Christian, but evil for good is devilish; it is so very absurd and wicked a thing that we cannot think but God will avenge it. See how great the evil was that they did against him: <hi type="italic">They have dug a pit for my soul;</hi> they aimed to take away his life (no less would satisfy them), and that not in a generous way, by an open assault, against which he might have an opportunity of defending himself, but in a base, cowardly, clandestine way: <hi type="italic">they dug pits for</hi> him, which there was no fence against, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.85">Ps. cxix. 85</reference>. But see how great the good was which he had done for them: <hi type="italic">Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them;</hi> he had been an intercessor with God for them, had used his interest in heaven on their behalf, which was the greatest kindness they could expect from one of his character. <hi type="italic">He is a prophet and he shall pray for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen. xx. 7</reference>. Moses often did this for Israel, and yet they quarrelled with him, and sometimes <hi type="italic">spoke of stoning him.</hi> He did them this kindness when they were in imminent danger of destruction and most needed it. They had themselves provoked God's wrath against them, and it was ready to break in upon them, but he stood in the gap (as Moses, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Ps. cvi. 23</reference>) <hi type="italic">and turned away</hi> that <hi type="italic">wrath.</hi> Now, (1.) This was very base in them. Call a man ungrateful and you can call him no worse. But it was not strange that those who had forgotten their God did not know their best friends. (2.) It was very grievous to him, as the like was to David. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Ps. xxxv. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">cix. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">For my love they are my adversaries.</hi> Thus disingenuously do sinners deal with the great intercessor, crucifying him afresh, and speaking against him on earth, while his blood is speaking for them in heaven. See <reference osisRef="John.10.32">John x. 32</reference>. But, (3.) It was a comfort to the prophet that, when they were so spiteful against him, he had the testimony of his conscience for him that he had done his duty to them; and the same will be our rejoicing in such a day of evil. <hi type="italic">The blood-thirsty hate the upright, but the just seek his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Prov. xxix. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen17622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17623" type="x-p"/> 3. He imprecates the judgments of God upon them, not from a revengeful disposition, but in a prophetical indignation against their horrid wickedness, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.21-Jer.18.23">v. 21-23</reference>. He prays, (1.) That their families might be starved for want of bread: "<hi type="italic">Deliver up the children to the famine,</hi> to the famine in the country for want of rain, and that in the city through the straitness of the siege. Thus let this iniquity of the fathers be visited upon the children." (2.) That they might be cut off <hi type="italic">by the sword</hi> of war, which, whatever it was in the enemy's hand, would be, in God's hand, a sword of justice: "<hi type="italic">Pour them out</hi> (so the word is) <hi type="italic">by the hands of the sword;</hi> let <hi type="italic">their blood</hi> be shed as profusely as water, that <hi type="italic">their wives</hi> may be left childless <hi type="italic">and widows,</hi> their husbands being taken away by <hi type="italic">death</hi>" (some think that the prophet refers to <hi type="italic">pestilence</hi>); <hi type="italic">let their young men,</hi> that are the strength of this generation and the hope of the next, <hi type="italic">be slain by the sword in battle.</hi> (3.) That the terrors and desolations of war might seize them suddenly and by surprise, that thus their punishment might answer to their sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let a cry be heard from their houses,</hi> loud shrieks, <hi type="italic">when thou shalt bring a troop</hi> of the Chaldeans <hi type="italic">suddenly upon them,</hi> to seize them and all they have, to make them prisoners and their estates a prey;" for thus they would have done by Jeremiah; they aimed to ruin him at once ere he was aware: "<hi type="italic">They have dug a pit</hi> for <hi type="italic">me,</hi> as for a wild beast, <hi type="italic">and</hi> have <hi type="italic">hid snares for</hi> me, as for some ravenous noxious fowl." Note, Those that think to ensnare others will justly be themselves ensnared in an evil time. (4.) That they might be dealt with according to the desert of this sin, which was without excuse: "<hi type="italic">Forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight;</hi> that is, let them not escape the just punishment of it; let them lie under all the miseries of those whose sins are unpardoned." (5.) That God's wrath against them might be their ruin: <hi type="italic">Let them be overthrown before thee.</hi> This intimates that justice was in pursuit of them, that they endeavoured to make their escape from it, but in vain; "they shall be made to stumble in their flight, and being overthrown they will certainly be overtaken." And then, Lord, <hi type="italic">in the time of thy anger,</hi> do to them (he does not say what he would have done to them, but) do to them as thou thinkest fit, as thou usest to do with those whom thou art angry with—<hi type="italic">deal thus with them.</hi> Now this is not written for our imitation. Jeremiah was a prophet, and by the impulse of the spirit of prophecy, in the foresight of the ruin certainly coming upon his persecutors, might pray such prayers as we may not; and, if we think by this example to justify ourselves in such imprecations, we <hi type="italic">know not what manner of spirit we are of;</hi> our Master has taught us, by his precept and pattern, to <hi type="italic">bless those that curse us and pray for those that despitefully use us.</hi> Yet it is written for our instruction, and is of use to teach us, [1.] That those who have forfeited the benefit of the prayers of God's prophets for them may justly expect to have their prayers against them. [2.] That persecution is a sin that fills the measure of a people's iniquity very fast, and will bring as sure and sore a destruction upon them as any thing. [3.] Those who will not be won upon by the kindness of God and his prophets will certainly at length feel the just resentments of both.  <chapter eID="Jer.18"/> <div eID="gen17623" type="x-p"/>

entries.e50105369fbdb87b3ce76d02d4d4fa3623c65fe8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9989"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.18.23">Jr 18:1-23</reference>. God, as the Sole Sovereign, Has an Absolute Right to Deal with Nations According to Their Conduct towards Him; Illustrated in a Tangible Form by the Potter's Moulding of Vessels from Clay.</title> <div sID="gen17781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9989"/><hi type="bold">2. go down--</hi>namely, from the high ground on which the temple stood, near which Jeremiah exercised his prophetic office, to the low ground, where some well-known (this is the force of "the") potter had his workshop. <div eID="gen17781" type="x-p"/>
entries.3302cff3166068ab205974092467981f5050ad38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9990"/><div sID="gen17782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9990"/><hi type="bold">3. wheels--</hi>literally, "on both stones." The potter's horizontal lathe consisted of two round plates, the lower one larger, the upper smaller; of stone originally, but afterwards of wood. On the upper the potter moulded the clay into what shapes he pleased. They are found represented in Egyptian remains. In <reference osisRef="Exod.1.16">Ex 1:16</reference> alone is the Hebrew word found elsewhere, but in a different sense. <div eID="gen17782" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ad3f19e4a107bab7130158749bb5daee17d1709: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9991"/><div sID="gen17783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9991"/><hi type="bold">4. marred--</hi>spoiled. "Of clay" is the true reading, which was corrupted into "as clay" (Margin), through the similarity of the two Hebrew letters, and from <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jr 18:6</reference>, "as the clay." <div eID="gen17783" type="x-p"/>
entries.588d23c65d6a5e86a6b08609d67a2bf2b2b0e266: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9992"/><div sID="gen17784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9992"/>6. Refuting the Jews' reliance on their external privileges as God's elect people, as if God could never cast them off. But if the potter, a mere creature, has power to throw away a marred vessel and raise up other clay from the ground, a fortiori God, the Creator, can cast away the people who prove unfaithful to His election and can raise others in their stead (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">64:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">21</reference>). It is curious that the potter's field should have been the purchase made with the price of Judas' treachery (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.10">10</reference>: a potter's vessel dashed to pieces, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>), because of its failing to answer the maker's design, being the very image to depict God's sovereign power to give reprobates to destruction, not by caprice, but in the exercise of His righteous judgment. Matthew quotes Zechariah's words (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference>) as Jeremiah's because the latter (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 18:1-19:15</reference>) was the source from which the former derived his summary in <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference> [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen17784" type="x-p"/>
entries.83405b893a35398815450dd90eb45efd6e54f7e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9993"/><div sID="gen17785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9993"/><hi type="bold">7. At what instant--</hi>in a moment, when the nation least expects it. Hereby he reminds the Jews how marvellously God had delivered them from their original degradation, that is, In one and the same day ye were the most wretched, and then the most favored of all people [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17785" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebb2b14fa577b01f48a7e71ee879592ad89948fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9994"/><div sID="gen17786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9994"/><hi type="bold">8. their evil--</hi>in antithesis to, "the evil that I thought to do."<div eID="gen17786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repent--</hi>God herein adapts Himself to human conceptions. The change is not in God, but in the circumstances which regulate God's dealings: just as we say the land recedes from us when we sail forth, whereas it is we who recede from the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.21">Eze 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.11">33:11</reference>). God's unchangeable principle is to do the best that can be done under all circumstances; if then He did not take into account the moral change in His people (their prayers, &c.), He would not be acting according to His own unchanging principle (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">Jr 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.10">10</reference>). This is applied practically to the Jews' case (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jr 18:11</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.26.3">Jr 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17787" type="x-p"/>
entries.dac1cb8f657c0fbe0b157f45aa9e5fdb452b8a59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9995"/><div sID="gen17788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9995"/><hi type="bold">11. frame evil--</hi>alluding to the preceding image of "the potter," that is, I, Jehovah, am now as it were the potter framing evil against you; but in the event of your repenting, it is in My power to frame anew My course of dealing towards you.<div eID="gen17788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13">2Ki 17:13</reference>). <div eID="gen17789" type="x-p"/>
entries.80bb6fdb93d7f8ad3163147631a89e1e4b6fe55c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9996"/><div sID="gen17790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9996"/><hi type="bold">12. no hope--</hi>Thy threats and exhortations are all thrown away (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>). Our case is desperate; we are hopelessly abandoned to our sins and their penalty. In this and the following clauses, "We will walk after our own devices," Jeremiah makes them express the real state of the case, rather than the hypocritical subterfuges which they would have been inclined to put forth. So <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Is 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.11">11</reference>. <div eID="gen17790" type="x-p"/>
entries.819d6d569f52ae93c2003faf45c94401cdf40b20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9997"/><div sID="gen17791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9997"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.10">Jr 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). Even among the heathen it was a thing unheard of, that a nation should lay aside its gods for foreign gods, though their gods are false gods. But Israel forsook the true God for foreign false gods.<div eID="gen17791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin of Israel--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">2Ki 19:21</reference>). It enhances their guilt, that Israel was the virgin whom God had specially betrothed to Him.<div eID="gen17792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horrible thing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.30">Jr 5:30</reference>). <div eID="gen17793" type="x-p"/>
entries.e68c8f52efa1ef48706bfc0e54fcbdfa6c958c9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9998"/><div sID="gen17794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9998"/>14. Is there any man (living near it) who would leave the snow of Lebanon (that is, the cool melted snow water of Lebanon, as he presently explains), which cometh from the rock of the field (a poetical name for Lebanon, which towers aloft above the surrounding field, or comparatively plain country)? None. Yet Israel forsakes Jehovah, the living fountain close at hand, for foreign broken cisterns. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jr 17:13</reference>; 2:13, accord with English Version here. Maurer translates, "Shall the snow of Lebanon cease from the rock to water (literally, 'forsake') My fields" (the whole land around being peculiarly Jehovah's)? Lebanon means the "white mountain"; so called from the perpetual snow which covers that part called Hermon, stretching northeast of Palestine.<div eID="gen17794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that come from another place--</hi>that come from far, namely, from the distant lofty rocks of Lebanon. Henderson translates, "the compressed waters," namely, contracted within a narrow channel while descending through the gorges of the rocks; "flowing" may in this view be rather "flowing down" (<reference osisRef="Song.4.15">So 4:15</reference>). But the parallelism in English Version is better, "which cometh from the rock," "that cometh from another place."<div eID="gen17795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be forsaken--</hi>answering to the parallel, "Will a man leave," &c. Maurer translates, "dry up," or "fail" (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>); the sense thus being, Will nature ever turn aside from its fixed course? The "cold waters" (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.25.25">Pr 25:25</reference>) refer to the perennial streams, fed from the partial melting of the snow in the hot weather. <div eID="gen17796" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2909d3679b0e9cc044e6830ab877d7120b58186: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9999"/><div sID="gen17797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9999"/><hi type="bold">15. Because--</hi>rather, "And yet"; in defiance of the natural order of things.<div eID="gen17797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgotten me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.32">Jr 2:32</reference>). This implies a previous knowledge of God, whereas He was unknown to the Gentiles; the Jews' forgetting of God, therefore, arose from determined perversity.<div eID="gen17798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they have caused ... to stumble--</hi>namely the false prophets and idolatrous priests have.<div eID="gen17799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancient paths--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jr 6:16</reference>): the paths which their pious ancestors trod. Not antiquity indiscriminately, but the example of the fathers who trod the right way, is here commended.<div eID="gen17800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them--</hi>the Jews.<div eID="gen17801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not cast up--</hi>not duly prepared: referring to the raised center of the road. Calvin translates, "not trodden." They had no precedent of former saints to induce them to devise for themselves a new worship. <div eID="gen17802" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5e37c6a56747518306245b68175dd2cc601fd0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10000"/><div sID="gen17803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10000"/><hi type="bold">16. hissing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>). In sign of contempt. That which was to be only the event is ascribed to the purpose of the people, although altogether different from what they would have been likely to hope for. Their purpose is represented as being the destruction of their country, because it was the inevitable result of their course of acting.<div eID="gen17803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wag ... head--</hi>in mockery (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">2Ki 19:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Mt 27:39</reference>). As "wag ... head" answers to "hissing," so "astonished" answers to "desolate," for which, therefore, Munster and others rather translate, "an object of wonder" (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.8">Jr 19:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17804" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad8c893a32201a5e626c3b84c84267ebc5c6cdaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10001"/><div sID="gen17805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10001"/><hi type="bold">17. as with an east wind--</hi>literally, "I will scatter them, as an east wind (scatters all before it)": a most violent wind (<reference osisRef="Job.27.21">Job 27:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>). Thirty-two manuscripts read (without as), "with an east wind."<div eID="gen17805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will show them the back ... not ... face--</hi>just retribution: as "they turned their back unto Me ... not their face" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>). <div eID="gen17806" type="x-p"/>
entries.12ddd9b1750029813145bf4cd811b2c10fc4f9ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10002"/><div sID="gen17807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10002"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jr 11:19</reference>). Let us bring a capital charge against him, as a false prophet; "for (whereas he foretells that this land shall be left without priests to teach the law, Mal 2:7; without scribes to explain its difficulties; and without prophets to reveal God's will), the law shall not perish from the prophet," &c.; since God has made these a lasting institution in His church, and the law declares they shall never perish (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.18">Le 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">10:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>) [Grotius].<div eID="gen17807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wise--</hi>scribes and elders joined to the priests. Perhaps they mean to say, we must have right on our side, in spite of Jeremiah's words against us and our prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.15">Jr 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">29:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.32">32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">5:31</reference>); "for the law shall not perish," &c. I prefer Grotius' explanation.<div eID="gen17808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... tongue--</hi>by a false accusation (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.3">64:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.19">50:19</reference>). "For the tongue" (Margin), that is, for his speaking against us. "In the tongue," that is, let us kill him, that he may speak no more against us [Castalio]. <div eID="gen17809" type="x-p"/>
entries.a12ac41d460dfa84787ff49974885047f1e7f65f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10003"/><div sID="gen17810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10003"/><hi type="bold">19. Give heed--</hi>contrasted with, "let us not give heed" (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jr 18:18</reference>). As they give no heed to me, do Thou, O Lord, give heed to me, and let my words at least have their weight with Thee. <div eID="gen17810" type="x-p"/>
entries.46941ba858d4789dcf5b2cf8571e02beb75d1ef4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10004"/><div sID="gen17811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10004"/>20. In the particulars here specified, Jeremiah was a type of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.25">Joh 15:25</reference>).<div eID="gen17811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my soul--</hi>my life; me (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.7">Psa 35:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I stood before thee ... to turn away thy wrath--</hi>so Moses (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference>). So Jesus Christ, the antitype of previous partial intercessors (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Is 59:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17813" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1562e7bcc979cfaa6e8cf650bad42664261e4a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10005"/><div sID="gen17814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10005"/><hi type="bold">21. pour out their blood by the force of the sword--</hi>literally, "by the hands of the sword." So <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.5">Eze 35:5</reference>. Maurer with Jerome translates, "deliver them over to the power of the sword." But compare <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>. In this prayer he does not indulge in personal revenge, as if it were his own cause that was at stake; but he speaks under the dictation of the Spirit, ceasing to intercede, and speaking prophetically, knowing they were doomed to destruction as reprobates; for those not so, he doubtless ceased not to intercede. We are not to draw an example from this, which is a special case.<div eID="gen17814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put to death--</hi>or, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>, "perish by the death plague" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men ... young men--</hi>Horsley distinguishes the former as married men past middle age; the latter, the flower of unmarried youth. <div eID="gen17816" type="x-p"/>
entries.17366801523b07b4e57050d6a043e33d5c62fdce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10006"/><div sID="gen17817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10006"/><hi type="bold">22. cry--</hi>by reason of the enemy bursting in: let their houses be no shelter to them in their calamities [Calvin].<div eID="gen17817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">digged ... pit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">Jr 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.6">Psa 57:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.85">119:85</reference>). <div eID="gen17818" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e6b810674200a465931a70da0658c37989da685: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10007"/><div sID="gen17819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10007"/><hi type="bold">23. forgive not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.109.9">Psa 109:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">10, 14</reference>).<div eID="gen17819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blot out--</hi>image from an account-book (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>).<div eID="gen17820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thee--</hi>Hypocrites suppose God is not near, so long as they escape punishment; but when He punishes, they are said to stand before Him, because they can no longer flatter themselves they can escape His eye (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deal thus--</hi>exert Thy power against them [Maurer].<div eID="gen17822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time of thine anger--</hi>Though He seems to tarry, His time shall come at last (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2Pe 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">10</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.18"/>

entries.9cdc2c25d4a566e613da17e8abf08bd2da8dd750: <div eID="gen29755" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29756" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29757" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29757" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29756" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29758" type="x-p"/> The type of the potter's vessel, and its signification, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.18.10">Jer 18:1-10</reference>. The inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem exhorted to repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jer 18:11</reference>; but on their refusal, (which is represented to be as unnatural as if a man should prefer the snowy Lebanon or barren rock to a fruitful plain, or other waters to the cool stream of the fountain), their destruction is predicted, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.12-Jer.18.17">Jer 18:12-17</reference>. In consequence of these plain reproofs and warnings of Jeremiah, a conspiracy is formed against him, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer 18:18</reference>. This leads him to appeal to God for his integrity, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.19">Jer 18:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">Jer 18:20</reference>; who puts a most dreadful curse in the mouth of his prophet, strongly indicative of the terrible fate of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.21-Jer.18.23">Jer 18:21-23</reference>. <div eID="gen29758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29759" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29760" type="x-p"/> The word which came to Jeremiah - This discourse is supposed to have been delivered some time in the reign of Jehoiakim, probably within the first three years.
entries.fe71bf0b716f7d11bc9fcfb1e484472eb64cfc2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29761" type="x-p"/> Go down to the potter's house - By this similitude God shows the absolute state of dependence on himself in which he has placed mankind. They are as clay in the hands of the potter; and in reference to every thing here below, he can shape their destinies as he pleases. Again; though while under the providential care of God they may go morally astray, and pervert themselves, yet they can be reclaimed by the almighty and all-wise Operator, and become such vessels as seemeth good for him to make. In considering this parable we must take heed that in running parallels we do not destroy the free agency of man, nor disgrace the goodness and supremacy of God.
entries.f34c7bdbe10fddd7a2634510c76f7132256e7cff: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29762" type="x-p"/> He wrought a work on the wheels - אל האבנים al haabnayim, upon the stones, the potter's wheel being usually made of such, the spindle of the moving stone being placed on a stone below, on which it turned, and supported the stone above, on which the vessel was manufactured, and which alone had a rotatory motion. The potter's wheel in the present day seems to differ very little from that which was in use between two and three thousand years ago.
entries.d4c5addcdfebebe9b8a3a9d19d983bd743a92e9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29763" type="x-p"/> The vessel - was marred in the hands of the potter - It did not stand in the working; it got out of shape; or some gravel or small stone having been incorporated with the mass of clay, made a breach in that part where it was found, so that the potter was obliged to knead up the clay afresh, place it on the wheel, and form it anew; and then it was such a vessel as seemed good to the potter to make it.
entries.04bcfa177b6c2b4c41b21dd250f8fc14a9cd65fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29764" type="x-p"/> Cannot I do with you as this potter? - Have I not a right to do with a people whom I have created as reason and justice may require? If they do not answer my intentions, may I not reject and destroy them; and act as this potter, make a new vessel out of that which at first did not succeed in his hands? <div eID="gen29764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29765" type="x-p"/> It is generally supposed that St. Paul has made a very different use of this similitude from that mentioned above. See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Rom 9:20</reference>, etc. His words are, "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honor, and another unto dishonor?" To this every sensible and pious man will answer, Undoubtedly he has. But would any potter make an exceedingly fair and good vessel on purpose to dash it to pieces when he had done? Surely no! And would or could, the God of infinite perfection and love make millions of immortal souls on purpose for eternal perdition, as the horrible decree of reprobation states? No! This is a lie against all the attributes of God. But does not the text state that he can, out of the same lump, the same mass of human nature, make one vessel to honor, and another to dishonor? Yes. But the text does not say, what the horrible decree says, that he makes one part, and indeed the greater, for eternal perdition. But what then is the meaning of the text? Why evidently this: As out of the same mass of clay a potter may make a flagon for the table and a certain utensil for the chamber, the one for a more honorable, the other for a less honorable use, though both equally necessary to the owner; so God, out of the same flesh and blood, may make the tiller of the field and the prophet of the Most High; the one in a more honorable, the other in a less honorable employ; yet both equally necessary in the world, and equally capable of bringing glory to God in their respective places. But if the vessel be marred in his hand, under his providential and gracious dealings, he may reject it as he did the Jews, and make another vessel, such as he is pleased with, of the Gentiles; yet even these marred vessels, the reprobate Jews, are not finally rejected; for all Israel shall be saved in (through) the Lord, i.e., Jesus Christ. And should the Gentiles act as the Jews have done, then they also shall be cut off, and God will call his Church by another name. See on <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom 9:22</reference> (note) and below.
entries.0e9aa8a49995a08c4f4a9c11ed0e811f72c21d16: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29766" type="x-p"/> At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, etc. - If that nation, against whom, etc. - And at what instant, etc. - If it do evil, etc. - These verses contain what may be called God's decree by which the whole of his conduct towards man is regulated. If he purpose destruction against an offending person, if that person repent and turn to God, he shall live and not die. If he purpose peace and salvation to him that walketh uprightly, if he turn from God to the world and sin, he shall die and not live.
entries.d2a0cf53ffba53ca7a1419c29a4ecb6ffe96b109: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29767" type="x-p"/> There is no hope - See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jer 2:25</reference>.
entries.680daa26c0e41444408b6f2aa91d7cc2e3250029: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29768" type="x-p"/> The virgin of Israel - Instead of ישראל Yisrael, three of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., with the Alexandrian copy of the Septuagint, have ירושלם Yerushalem, Jerusalem.
entries.b4f1239becfc3e9165a734a3d9285ed8fcdba00f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29769" type="x-p"/> Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon - Lebanon was the highest mountain in Judea. Would any man in his senses abandon a farm that was always watered by the melted snows of Lebanon, and take a barren rock in its place? How stupid therefore and absurd are my people, who abandon the everlasting God for the worship of idols!
entries.2472f92713647a0c2bf6e5be00ed550c33d5e031: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29770" type="x-p"/> A perpetual hissing - שריקות sherikoth. a shrieking, hissing; an expression of contempt.
entries.a3d91f018ec0fbb7dcaaa959ef1f77c5d870a27c: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29771" type="x-p"/> I will scatter them as with an east wind - It is the property of this wind, almost every where, to parch up, blast, and destroy grain and trees, and even cattle and men suffer from it. Hence the old metrical proverb: - "When the wind blows from the east, 'Tis good for neither man nor beast."
entries.9490e8d2e14d394e5323aa293946c2020c703104: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29772" type="x-p"/> Come, and let us devise devices - Let us form a conspiracy against him, accuse him of being a false prophet, and a contradicter of the words of God, for God has promised us protection, and he says we shall be destroyed, and that God will forsake his people. <div eID="gen29772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29773" type="x-p"/> Let us smite him with the tongue - On the tongue; so it should be rendered. Lying and false testimony are punished in the eastern countries, to the present day, by smiting the person on the mouth with a strong piece of leather like the sole of a shoe. Sometimes a bodkin is run through the tongue. Blasphemy, calumny, and cursing of parents, are usually punished in that way among the Chinese.
entries.31bad372e203beb03f4c8cb79fad0b7a8f3aa817: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29774" type="x-p"/> They have digged a pit for my soul - For my life; this they wish to take away. <div eID="gen29774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29775" type="x-p"/> Stood before thee to speak good for them - I was their continual intercessor.
entries.e24e7fe6f5eb01527b8dfaf8fb8fb318e23a83a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29776" type="x-p"/> Therefore deliver up their children - The execrations in these verses should be considered as simply prophetic declarations of the judgments which God was about to pour out on them. <div eID="gen29776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29777" type="x-p"/> If we consider them in their grammatical meaning, then they are not directions to us to whom our Lawgiver has said, "Love your enemies."  <chapter eID="Jer.18"/> <div eID="gen29777" type="x-p"/>

entries.17ad42016f7d2e3b70a14e471f1cdc89dfe58e1e: <reference osisRef="Jer.18.1">Jer 18:1</reference> <div eID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> The Emblem of the Clay and the Potter and the Complaint of the Prophet against his Adversaries. - The figure of the potter who remodels a misshapen vessel (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.2-Jer.18.4">Jer 18:2-4</reference>). The interpretation of this (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.5-Jer.18.10">Jer 18:5-10</reference>), and its application to degenerate Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11-Jer.18.17">Jer 18:11-17</reference>). The reception of the discourse by the people, and Jeremiah’s cry to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.18-Jer.18.23">Jer 18:18-23</reference>).
entries.92e0da4b857ea7de3f22c84735d0fefb13eb690f: <reference osisRef="Jer.18.2-Jer.18.5">Jer 18:2-5</reference> <hi type="italic">The emblem and its interpretation. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.2">Jer 18:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Arise and go down into the potter’s house; there will I cause thee to hear my words.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.3">Jer 18:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I went down into the potter’s house; and, behold, he wrought on the wheels.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.4">Jer 18:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. And the vessel was marred, that he wrought in clay, in the hand of the potter; then he made again another vessel of it, as seemed good to the potter to make.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.5">Jer 18:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. Then came the word of Jahveh to me, saying:</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jer 18:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. Cannot I do with you as this potter, house of Israel? saith Jahveh. Behold, as the clay in the hand of the potter, so are ye in mine hand, house of Israel.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jer 18:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. Now I speak concerning a people and kingdom, to root it out and pluck up and destroy it.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.8">Jer 18:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. But if that people turns from its wickedness, against which I spake, the it repents me of the evil which I thought to do it.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.9">Jer 18:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. And now I speak concerning a people and a kingdom, to build and to plant it.</hi> Jer 18:10. <hi type="italic">If it do that which is evil in mine eyes, so that it hearkens not unto my voice, then it repents me of the good which I said I would do unto it."</hi> <div eID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> By God’s command Jeremiah is to go and see the potter’s treatment of the clay, and to receive thereafter God’s interpretation of the same. Here he has set before his eyes that which suggests a comparison of man to the clay and of God to the potter, a comparison that frequently occurred to the Hebrews, and which had been made to appear in the first formation of man (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.10.9">Job 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Isa 29:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">Isa 64:7</reference>). This is done that he may forcibly represent to the people, by means of the emblem, the power of the Lord to do according to His will with all nations, and so with Israel too. From the "go down," we gather that the potteries of Jerusalem lay in a valley near the city. האבנים are the round frames by means of which the potter moulded his vessels. This sig. of the word is well approved here; but in <reference osisRef="Exod.1.16">Exo 1:16</reference>, where too it is found, the meaning is doubtful, and it is a question whether the derivation is from אבן or from אופן, wheel. The <hi type="italic">perfecta consec</hi>. ונשׁחת and ושׁב designate, taken in connection with the participle עשׂה, actions that were possibly repeated: "and if the vessel was spoilt, he made it over again;" cf. Ew. §342, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. עשׂה , working in clay, of the material in which men work in order to make something of it; cf. Exo 31:4.<note placement="foot">Instead of בּחמר several <hi type="italic">codd</hi>. and <hi type="italic">editt</hi>. have כּחמר, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jer 18:6</reference>, to which Ew. and Hitz. both take objection, so that they delete כחמר (Ew.) or כּחמר בּיד היּוצר (Hitz.) as being glosses, since the words are not in the lxx. The attempts of Umbr. and Nag. to obtain a sense for כּחמר are truly of such a kind as only to strengthen the suspicion of spuriousness. Umbr., who is followed by Graf, expounds: "as the clay in the hand of the potter does;" whereto Hitz. justly replies: "but is then the (failure) solely its own doing?" Näg. will have כ to be the כ <hi type="italic">verit</hi>.: the vessel was marred, as clay in the hand of the potter, in which case the כחמר still interrupts. But the failure of the attempts to make a good sense of כחמר does in no respect justify the uncritical procedure of Ew. and Hitz. in deleting the word without considering that the reading is by no means established, since not only do the most important and correct editions and a great number of <hi type="italic">codd</hi>. read בּחמר, but Aquila, Theodot., the Chald, and Syr. give this reading; Norzi and Houbig. call it <hi type="italic">lectio accuratiorum codicum</hi>, and the Masora on <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jer 18:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.10.9">Job 10:9</reference> confirms it. Cf. de Rossi <hi type="italic">variae lectt. ad h. l</hi>. and the critical remarks in the <hi type="italic">Biblia Hal</hi>. by J. H. Michaelis, according to which כחמר plainly made its way into the present verse from <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jer 18:6</reference> by the error of a copyist; and it can only be from his prejudice in favour of the lxx that Hitz. pronounces כחמר original, as being "the reading traditionally in use."</note>
entries.b9d15ceb11b8549b40be444937ff35ab298c6c53: <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6-Jer.18.10">Jer 18:6-10</reference> <div eID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14050" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6-Jer.18.10">Jer 18:6-10</reference> the Lord discloses to the prophet the truth lying in the potter’s treatment of the clay.
